name: Kanuri (Kolofata)
overview: In the majority in Kolofata, the Kanuri live there with the Mandara, Podoko, Mouktélé, Gamergou, Shuwa Arabs and Fulani. Coming from Yemen via Kouka and Maiduguri, these heirs of Bornu organise their lives around kingship, Islam and occupational castes (blacksmiths, butchers, weavers, tailors); farming, small livestock rearing and trade provide their living.

sections.title: Identity and neighbours
items: Majority and open group, whose members also speak the languages of their neighbours.
Kanuri is also spoken in Nigeria and Chad.
Marriages unite natives and non-natives; men especially take wives from other groups.

sections.title: Territory and migrations
items: The Kanuri occupy the land of their ancestors, marked by the memory of the sheikh who founded Islam there.
Having set out from Yemen, they stayed at Kouka and Maiduguri, with which they keep ties.

sections.title: Social organisation and power
items: Kingship and kinship organise society; decisions, made as a group, are issued by the chief.
Children talk freely with their parents; the woman avoids interactions with men.
Occupational castes: blacksmiths (hoes, knives), butchers, weavers, tailors.

sections.title: Kinship, marriage and life passages
items: Patrilineal kinship; the wife joins her husband's family.
Today, it is the young man who chooses his partner; then come the meeting and the parents' request.
Bride price and gifts symbolise the engagement and announce the marriage, the kola serves as testimony, and animals are slaughtered to receive the guests.

sections.title: Beliefs, sacred places and taboos
items: Religious life is Islamic: neighbourhood mosque (machidi) and prayer ground outside the village (yidi kmandze), which keeps the memory of the group.
Birth is a joy that enlarges the family; death is a loss. After the five prayers, people pray for the deceased: these prayers nourish them.
Taboos: talking about sexuality, theft, disorder; prohibitions: theft, adultery, insults.
Serious offences (adultery, crime, theft, desecration) lead to a fine, ostracism or prison.
People rely on prayer led by the imam, on sacrifices and on fasting.

sections.title: Economy, land and crafts
items: Men: farming, small-scale livestock rearing, trade, hunting. Women: trade, hairdressing, farming.
The land belongs to the village chief; it is accessed through the neighbourhood chief.
Ancestral crafts: mats, shoes, clothing, hats made of rônier palm leaves against the sun.

sections.title: Clothing, health, beauty
items: Men: sleeveless gandoura, grand boubou with long sleeves, waistcoat. Women: three-piece wrapper, kaba.
Traditional medicine remains widely used: effective and accessible.
Beauty: figure and elegance; for women, adornment and beautiful hair.
Courtship: dancing talent, conversation and gifts, on both sides.

sections.title: Music, dances and festivals
items: Rhythms: bala (tam-tam, drum, fiddle), guara (drum, flute, fiddle, guitar), ganga koura, gourldi.
Dances: agaita at weddings, kourmi at chiefdom ceremonies, ganga koura at nuptials, bala reserved for the wedding of the chief's daughter.
Festivals: Mouloud, Ramadan, Tabaski.

sections.title: History and cultural kinship
items: The Kanuri share their migration route and many traditions with the Mandara and the Gamergou, including facial scarification.

sections.title: The names
items: Names depend on sex and circumstances; people do not change their name, but out of respect one avoids calling an elder by name.
Appellatives: Abba, Yandzié, Yagana, Modou, Bana, Yakoura, Zara, Awana.
The founding ancestor, Yaman, refers to the “people of Yemen”.

lessons.title: Who are the Kanuri (Kolofata)? Identity, language and territory
objectives: Name the Kanuri (Kolofata) community and explain its name
Locating your territory and its neighbours
Telling one's origin according to tradition
lessons.competence: Introduce the Kanuri (Kolofata) community (name, language, territory, neighbours, origin) and place it within the cultural diversity of Cameroon.
lessons.situation: A pen pal from another region asks you to introduce the Kanuri (Kolofata) community to them: who are they, where do they live, where do they come from?
lessons.materiel: Map of Cameroon, cultural profile of the community (“Cultures” section of Likalo).

teacher.intro: Expected competence: Present the Kanuri (Kolofata) community (name, language, territory, neighbours, origin) and place it within Cameroon's cultural diversity.

steps.title: Discovering the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Write the situation on the board and have it read: “A pen friend from another region asks you to introduce the Kanuri (Kolofata) community to them: who are they, where do they live, where do they come from?” The students think individually.

steps.title: Working on the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Questions to guide the analysis: — What do the Kanuri (Kolofata) call themselves and what does this name mean? — What language do they speak, and where else is it spoken? — Which peoples do they live with? — Where did they come from, according to tradition?

steps.title: Sharing and comparing the results (5 min)
steps.instruction: Compare the groups' answers, keep the correct proposals on the board and identify what the class does not yet know.

steps.title: Mobilising resources (20 min)
steps.instruction: Present, or have the students discover, the following: • Majority and open group, whose members also speak the languages of their neighbours. • Kanuri is also spoken in Nigeria and Chad. • Marriages unite indigenous people and outsiders; men especially take wives from other groups. • The Kanuri occupy the land of their ancestors, marked by the memory of the sheikh who founded Islam there. • Having left Yemen, they stayed at Kouka and Maiduguri, with which they keep ties.

steps.title: Consolidating what has been learned — written summary (5 min)
steps.instruction: In the majority in Kolofata, the Kanuri live there with the Mandara, Podoko, Mouktélé, Gamergou, Shuwa Arabs and Fulani. Coming from Yemen via Kouka and Maiduguri, these heirs of Bornu organise their lives around kingship, Islam and occupational castes (blacksmiths, butchers, weavers, tailors); farming, small livestock rearing and trade provide their living.

steps.title: Assessment of learning (10 min)
steps.instruction: On a map of Cameroon, locate the Kanuri (Kolofata) community and its neighbours, then write 5 sentences to introduce it to your pen pal.

steps.title: Remediation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Correct together; with students who are struggling, go back over a single element of the written summary, using a concrete example from their own community.

teacher.freedom: Some knowledge (rites, sacred places, initiate societies) is restricted: in class, only what the community makes public is covered, with respect and without judgement. Compare with the students' own culture.
teacher.tips: Approach recommended by the National Cultures teaching guide: active and participatory methods (“learning by doing”). If possible, invite a resource person from the community, or propose a survey of the elders.

lessons.title: Power and social organisation among the Kanuri (Kolofata)
lessons.anelcac: Socio-political organisation, rules for living together
lessons.competence: Describe how the Kanuri (Kolofata) organise power, make decisions and regulate community life.
lessons.situation: An important decision must be made for the whole Kanuri (Kolofata) village. Who decides, and how?
lessons.materiel: The community's cultural profile, paper and felt-tip pens for the organisation chart.

teacher.intro: Expected competence: Describe how the Kanuri (Kolofata) organise power, make decisions and regulate community life.

steps.title: Discovering the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Write the situation on the board and have it read: “An important decision has to be made for the whole Kanuri (Kolofata) village. Who decides, and how?” The students think individually.

steps.title: Working on the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Questions to guide the analysis: — Who holds authority? — How are decisions made (consensus, vote, the chief's decision)? — What rules of respect and deference are observed? — Which groups or societies play a particular role?

steps.title: Sharing and comparing the results (5 min)
steps.instruction: Compare the groups' answers, keep the correct proposals on the board and identify what the class does not yet know.

steps.title: Mobilising resources (20 min)
steps.instruction: Present, or have the students discover, the following points: • Kingship and kinship organise society; decisions, taken as a group, are issued by the chief. • Children exchange freely with their parents; the woman avoids interactions with men. • Craft castes: blacksmiths (hoes, knives), butchers, weavers, tailors.

steps.title: Consolidating what has been learned — written summary (5 min)
steps.instruction: Kingship and kinship organise society; decisions, made as a group, are issued by the chief. Children talk freely with their parents; the woman avoids interactions with men. Trade castes: blacksmiths (hoes, knives), butchers, weavers, tailors.

steps.title: Assessment of learning (10 min)
steps.instruction: Draw a diagram (organisation chart) of power among the Kanuri (Kolofata), then explain in 3 sentences how a decision is made.

steps.title: Remediation (5 min)

lessons.moduleTitle: Module C-II — Cultural practices: ways of life
lessons.title: Traditional food and drink of the Kanuri (Kolofata)
objectives: Linking food to the living environment

vocabulary.langText: boule de mil rouge et de sorgho

lessons.competence: Identify the traditional dishes and drinks of the Kanuri (Kolofata), describe how they are prepared and bring out their cultural significance.
lessons.situation: Your class is preparing a food fair. Your group must present a traditional dish of the Kanuri (Kolofata).
lessons.materiel: Cultural profile, pictures or local ingredients, display materials.

teacher.intro: Expected competence: Identify the traditional foods and drinks of the Kanuri (Kolofata), describe their preparation and bring out their cultural significance.

steps.title: Discovering the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Write the situation on the board and have it read: “Your class is preparing a food fair. Your group has to present a traditional dish of the Kanuri (Kolofata).” The students think individually.

steps.title: Working on the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Questions to guide the analysis: — What are the main dishes and drinks? — What products are they made from? Where do these products come from? — Who prepares them, and on what occasions? — What do they say about the community's living environment?

steps.title: Sharing and comparing the results (5 min)
steps.instruction: Compare the groups' answers, keep the correct proposals on the board and identify what the class does not yet know.

steps.title: Mobilising resources (20 min)
steps.instruction: Present, or have the students discover, the following: • Traditional dishes: red millet and sorghum balls, fonio, beans, okra, leafy greens. • Drinks: porridge, tea. • Men: farming, small livestock rearing, trade, hunting. Women: trade, hairdressing, farming.

steps.title: Consolidating what has been learned — written summary (5 min)
steps.instruction: The Kanuri (Kolofata) eat mainly red millet balls and sorghum, fonio, beans, okra. Traditional drinks: porridge, tea. These foods are linked to the group's activities and to the products of its environment.

steps.title: Assessment of learning (10 min)
steps.instruction: Choose a dish of the Kanuri (Kolofata): write its sheet (name in the language, ingredients, steps, occasion when it is served).

steps.title: Remediation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Correct together; with students who are struggling, go back over a single element of the written summary, using a concrete example from their own community.

teacher.freedom: Some knowledge (rites, sacred places, initiate societies) is restricted: in class, only what the community makes public is covered, with respect and without judgement. Compare with the students' own culture.
teacher.tips: Approach recommended by the National Cultures teaching guide: active and participatory methods (“learning by doing”). If possible, invite a resource person from the community, or propose a survey of the elders.

steps.title: Working on the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Questions to guide the analysis: — What does a birth mean for the community? — Who gives the name, when and how? — Can the name change during a lifetime? — When and how does one become a man or a woman?

steps.title: Sharing and comparing the results (5 min)

After the five prayers, prayers are said for the dead: these prayers nourish them. • Patrilineal kinship; the wife joins her husband's family.

student.memo: Among the Kanuri (Kolofata), traditional dances (agaita, kourmi, bala) accompany the great moments of life: celebrations, mourning, weddings, initiations. Instruments: tam-tam, drum, fiddle, flute. Festival(s): Mouloud, Ramadan.

lessons.moduleTitle: Module C-IV — Cultural practices in communities (Level I)
lessons.title: Traditional economy and access to land among the Kanuri (Kolofata)
lessons.competence: Describe the economic activities of the Kanuri (Kolofata), the division of tasks between men and women and the rules of access to land.
lessons.situation: A development project wants to help the Kanuri (Kolofata). First it must understand how they work and who owns the land.

teacher.intro: Expected competence: Describe the economic activities of the Kanuri (Kolofata), the division of tasks between men and women and the rules of access to land.

steps.title: Discovering the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Write the situation on the board and have it read: “A development project wants to help the Kanuri (Kolofata). First it must understand how they work and who owns the land.” The students think individually.

steps.title: Working on the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Questions to guide the analysis: — What are the activities of men? of women? — Who owns the land and how is it accessed? — Which products are sold or exchanged? — Have these activities changed?

steps.title: Sharing and comparing the results (5 min)
steps.instruction: Compare the groups' answers, keep the correct proposals on the board and identify what the class does not yet know.

steps.title: Mobilising resources (20 min)
steps.instruction: Present the following points, or have the students discover them: • Men: farming, small livestock, trade, hunting. Women: trade, hairdressing, farming. • Land belongs to the village chief; access is through the quarter head. • Ancestral crafts: mats, shoes, clothes, hats made of palmyra palm leaves against the sun.

steps.title: Consolidating what has been learned — written summary (5 min)
steps.instruction: Men: farming, small-scale livestock rearing, trade, hunting. Women: trade, hairdressing, farming. Land belongs to the village chief; it is accessed through the quarter head.

steps.title: Assessment of learning (10 min)
steps.instruction: Draw a two-column table (men / women) of the Kanuri (Kolofata)'s activities, then explain how land is accessed.

steps.title: Remediation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Correct together; with students who are struggling, go back over a single element of the written summary, using a concrete example from their own community.

teacher.freedom: Some knowledge (rites, sacred places, initiate societies) is restricted: in class, only what the community makes public is covered, with respect and without judgement. Compare with the students' own culture.
teacher.tips: Approach recommended by the National Cultures teaching guide: active and participatory methods (“learning by doing”). If possible, invite a resource person from the community, or propose a survey of the elders.

lessons.moduleTitle: Module C-V — Cultural practices in communities (Level II)
lessons.title: Beliefs, sacred places and taboos among the Kanuri (Kolofata)
objectives: Explain beliefs about life and death
lessons.competence: Explain the beliefs, sacred places and taboos of the Kanuri (Kolofata), and their role in regulating social life.
lessons.situation: A visitor arrives among the Kanuri (Kolofata). Which places and which rules must he absolutely respect?

teacher.intro: Expected competence: Explain the beliefs, sacred places and taboos of the Kanuri (Kolofata), and their role in regulating social life.

steps.title: Discovering the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Write the situation on the board and have it read: “A visitor arrives among the Kanuri (Kolofata). Which places and which rules must they absolutely respect?” The students think individually.

steps.title: Working on the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Questions to guide the analysis: — What are the beliefs about birth and death? — Which places are sacred, and why? — What are the main taboos, and for whom? — How were serious offences atoned for?

steps.title: Sharing and comparing the results (5 min)
steps.instruction: Compare the groups' answers, keep the correct proposals on the board and identify what the class does not yet know.

steps.title: Mobilising resources (20 min)
steps.instruction: Present, or have the students discover, the following: • Religious life is Islamic: neighbourhood mosque (machidi) and prayer ground outside the village (yidi kmandze), which keeps the memory of the group. • Birth is a joy that enlarges the family; death is a loss. After the five prayers, people pray for the dead: these prayers nourish them. • Taboos: talking about sexuality, theft, disorder; prohibitions: theft, adultery, insult. • Serious offences (adultery, crime, theft, desecration) lead to a fine, exclusion or prison. • People rely on prayer guided by the imam, on sacrifices and on fasting.

steps.title: Consolidating what has been learned — written summary (5 min)
steps.instruction: Religious life is Islamic: neighbourhood mosque (machidi) and prayer ground outside the village (yidi kmandze), which keeps the memory of the group. Birth is a joy that enlarges the family; death is a loss. After the five prayers, people pray for the dead: these prayers nourish them.

steps.title: Assessment of learning (10 min)
steps.instruction: Write a short guide to good conduct for a visitor among the Kanuri (Kolofata) (3 places or rules to respect, with their reason).

steps.title: Remediation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Correct together; with students who are struggling, go back over a single element of the written summary, using a concrete example from their own community.

teacher.freedom: Some knowledge (rites, sacred places, initiate societies) is restricted: in class, only what the community makes public is covered, with respect and without judgement. Compare with the students' own culture.
teacher.tips: Approach recommended by the National Cultures teaching guide: active and participatory methods (“learning by doing”). If possible, invite a resource person from the community, or propose a survey of the elders.

lessons.moduleTitle: Module C-V — Cultural practices in communities (Level II)
lessons.title: Greeting, introducing yourself and counting in Kanuri
lessons.anelcac: Traditional media and transmission: everyday language
objectives: Greeting according to the time of day

vocabulary.frenchText: morning greetings (as a sign of deference/respect)

lessons.competence: Use the greeting and introduction formulas of the Kanuri (Kolofata) and count from 1 to 10, respecting customs.
lessons.situation: You are visiting a Kanuri (Kolofata) family. Greet them, introduce yourself and take part in the sharing of kola nuts by counting.
lessons.materiel: Cultural profile (“Common expressions” and “Counting” sections), kola nuts or small objects.

teacher.intro: Expected competence: Use the Kanuri (Kolofata) greeting and introduction formulas and count from 1 to 10, respecting customary usage.

steps.title: Discovering the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Write the situation on the board and have it read: “You are visiting a Kanuri (Kolofata) family. Greet them, introduce yourself and take part in the sharing of the cola nuts by counting.” The students think individually.

steps.title: Working on the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Questions to guide the analysis: — How do you greet people depending on the time of day? — How do you introduce yourself (name, origin, place of residence)? — How do you count from 1 to 10? Is the system decimal, vigesimal…? — Why is language a tool of transmission?

steps.title: Sharing and comparing the results (5 min)
steps.instruction: Compare the groups' answers, keep the correct proposals on the board and identify what the class does not yet know.

steps.title: Mobilising resources (20 min)
steps.instruction: Present the following points, or have the students discover them: • The community's language is Kanuri. • Greeting formulae: Saléfagna = Hello (neutral greeting, at any time of day); ndawatou = morning greeting (one person); ndawatoundo = morning greeting (several people). • Counting from 1 to 5: Lakka/fal, Indi, Yake, Dio, Où. • The founding ancestor, Yaman, refers to the “people of Yemen”. • The Kanuri share their migration route and many traditions with the Mandara and the Gamergou, including facial scarification.

steps.title: Consolidating what has been learned — written summary (5 min)
steps.instruction: Greeting and counting in Kanuri are the first steps towards communicating with the Kanuri (Kolofata). The polite expressions convey the respect owed to people according to the time of day and their rank.

steps.title: Assessment of learning (10 min)
steps.instruction: Role play in pairs: greet each other, introduce yourselves, ask where the other person comes from and count objects from 1 to 10.

steps.title: Remediation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Correct together; with students who are struggling, go back over a single element of the written summary, using a concrete example from their own community.

teacher.freedom: Some knowledge (rites, sacred places, initiate societies) is restricted: in class, only what the community makes public is covered, with respect and without judgement. Compare with the students' own culture.
teacher.tips: Approach recommended by the National Cultures teaching guide: active and participatory methods (“learning by doing”). If possible, invite a resource person from the community, or propose a survey of the elders.

student.intro: Learn to greet, introduce yourself and count in Kanuri.

activities.title: I greet
activities.instruction: Learn the greeting formulas for morning, midday and evening.

activities.title: I introduce myself
activities.instruction: Say your name, where you are from and where you live.

activities.title: I count
activities.instruction: Count objects from 1 to 10.

activities.title: I pass on
activities.instruction: Teach a formula to a classmate or a family member.

student.memo: Greeting and counting in Kanuri are the first steps towards communicating with the Kanuri (Kolofata). The polite expressions convey the respect owed to people according to the time of day and their rank.
